pos: n. (the Jesuit casuistry that a man may follow a probable opinion even when the contrary is more probable)
etymology: From Latin probabilis, that may be proved or approved. Bartholomew de Medina (1577) and the Jesuit moralists after him taught that if a competent doctor holds an opinion as probable, the penitent may follow it against a safer or more probable opinion. The 1689's answer is not a rival casuistry. It is a conscience bound by Scripture.
biblical_def: Probabilism is a rule for acting when doctors disagree. Scripture's rule is not the probable doctor. It is the clear word, and the doubting conscience. “And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin” (Rom 14:23). Paul will not let a man approve himself by a looser opinion: “Happy is he that condemneth not himself in that thing which he alloweth” (Rom 14:22). The test is what is acceptable to the Lord: “Proving what is acceptable unto the Lord” (Eph 5:10). And the standard is already written: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). James will not let the double-minded man treat hesitation as a permission: “A double minded man is unstable in all his ways” (Jas 1:8). A probable opinion that lets you do what you already wanted is not faith. It is a receipt.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines probable as likely, and probability as likelihood. Probabilism is the later Jesuit system that makes a likely opinion enough to act against a safer one.
webster_full: PROBABLE, a. [L. probabilis, from probo, to prove.]
Likely; having more evidence than the contrary, or evidence that inclines the mind to belief, but leaves some room for doubt.
PROBABILITY, n. Likelihood; appearance of truth.
PROBABILISM, in later casuistry, the rule that a probable opinion may be followed even against a more probable.
scriptures: And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin.
Hast thou faith? have it to thyself before God. Happy is he that condemneth not himself in that thing which he alloweth.
Eph 5:10
Proving what is acceptable unto the Lord.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Jas 1:8
A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.
corruption_summary: A probable doctor is made the judge of a doubtful act, and Paul makes faith the judge, and the law the light.
corruption_paragraphs: The Jesuit usefulness of probabilism is obvious. If five approved men say a thing may be done, the penitent may do it, even if ten say it may not. The conscience is no longer bound to the safest reading of the command. It is bound to the existence of a respectable loophole. Romans 14:23 does not ask whether a doctor can be cited. It asks whether the eater eats of faith. Whatsoever is not of faith is sin.

Isaiah 8:20 is why a church cannot outsource this to a faculty. To the law and to the testimony. If they speak not according to this word, there is no light in them. A probable opinion that cannot survive that sentence is not probable in any sense that should move a Christian.

The Protestant corruption is the same machine without the Latin. A man finds a podcast that blesses what his church still names as sin, and calls the disagreement complexity. Ephesians 5:10 is proving what is acceptable unto the Lord, not proving what a platform will tolerate. Casuistry is already on this shelf. Probabilism is the rule that made casuistry a market.
roots_summary: Latin probabilis, from probo, to prove; Greek dokimazo (G1381), to prove, test; pistis (G4102), faith.
roots_lines: Latin probabilismus — Medina, then the Jesuit moralists; a probable opinion suffices.
Greek pistis (G4102) — faith; Romans 14:23, whatsoever is not of faith is sin.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to prove; Ephesians 5:10, proving what is acceptable unto the Lord.
usage: “Whatsoever is not of faith is sin” — not, whatsoever a doctor will sign.
“To the law and to the testimony” — the only probable light.
“Proving what is acceptable unto the Lord” — not unto a faculty.

pos: n. phrase (sins a lower priest may not absolve, reserved to the bishop or the pope)
etymology: From the Latin canonical phrase casus reservati. Rome ranked certain sins as too grave or too public for ordinary absolution. The reservation is a claim about the keys: that forgiveness can be held upstream of the man who hears the confession. The New Testament's keys are not a schedule of withheld pardons.
biblical_def: Reserved cases are sins a parish priest is not allowed to clear. Scripture's forgiveness is not graded that way. “Who can forgive sins but God only?” (Mar 2:7), and the Son of man proves He can: “But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power on earth to forgive sins” (Mar 2:10). The apostolic ministry proclaims that forgiveness; it does not ration it by rank: “Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them” (John 20:23). John puts the ordinary path in one verse: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1Jn 1:9). And the church's discipline is for impenitence, not for a list the curate may not touch: “To whom ye forgive any thing, I forgive also” (2Co 2:10). A see that reserves pardon has already answered 1 John 1:9 with a queue.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines reserve as to keep in store, and reserved as kept for another. Reserved cases are sins Rome keeps for a higher absolution than the parish priest may give.
webster_full: RESERVE, v.t. [L. reservo; re and servo, to keep.]
To keep in store for future or other use; to withhold from present use.
RESERVED, a. Kept for another or future use; restrained from freedom of words or actions.
RESERVED CASES, in canon law, sins whose absolution is withheld from the ordinary priest.
scriptures: Mar 2:7
Why doth this man thus speak blasphemies? who can forgive sins but God only?
Mar 2:10
But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power on earth to forgive sins, (he saith to the sick of the palsy,)
John 20:23
Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
To whom ye forgive any thing, I forgive also: for if I forgave any thing, to whom I forgave it, for your sakes forgave I it in the person of Christ;
corruption_summary: Pardon is made a scarce good a higher chair controls, and John says He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins.
corruption_paragraphs: The pastoral excuse is order: some sins scandalize, and a bishop should handle them. Second Corinthians 2:10 is order without a reservation list. Forgiveness in the church is for the penitent, and Paul joins it, he does not withhold it until Rome stamps the case. Discipline that refuses the impenitent is biblical. Discipline that tells a broken man his sin is above his priest's pay grade is a different machine.

Mark 2 is why the machine cannot be baptized. Who can forgive sins but God only? The Son of man has power on earth to forgive sins. A hierarchy that then re-grades which sins may be spoken clean by which employee has put the keys back into a caste. John 20:23 is a commission to announce the gospel's remission, not a franchise agreement.

First John 1:9 is the sentence reserved cases exist to complicate. If we confess, He is faithful and just to forgive and to cleanse from all unrighteousness. All. A church that has a remainder the local minister may not touch has added a remainder John did not write. Confession-auricular is already on this shelf. This page is the lock on that box.
roots_summary: Latin casus reservati; Greek aphiemi (G863), to forgive, remit; homologeo (G3670), to confess.
roots_lines: Latin casus reservati — cases reserved to a superior for absolution.
Greek aphiemi (G863) — to send away, forgive; Mark 2:10, power to forgive sins; John 20:23, remit.
Greek homologeo (G3670) — to confess; 1 John 1:9, if we confess our sins.
usage: “Who can forgive sins but God only” — the question reserved cases re-open.
“Faithful and just to forgive” — and to cleanse from all.
“To whom ye forgive any thing” — Paul did not wait for a reserved list.

pos: n. (members of the Society of Jesus; in Protestant controversy, the order known for casuistry, equivocation, and the defence of papal power)
etymology: From Jesus, the Society of Jesus, founded by Ignatius of Loyola (1540). Webster already records both the member and the later English use: a crafty person, an intriguer. The dictionary uses the word for the order as the Reformation met it, not for every man who ever wore the cloth.
biblical_def: Jesuits are an order. The controversy is a method. Scripture already has a name for religion that wins by craft. “And through covetousness shall they with feigned words make merchandise of you” (2Pe 2:3). Paul feared the serpent's subtlety toward the church's mind: “But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ” (2Co 11:3). The Lord asked for a yes that stays yes: “But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil” (Mat 5:37). Jeremiah had already met the preacher of peace who had not been sent: “They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace” (Jer 6:14). And the test of the spirits is not the badge: “Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jn 4:1). An order named for Jesus is not thereby simple in Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Jesuit as a member of the Society of Jesus, and, in English usage, a crafty person, an intriguer; Jesuitical as designing, cunning.
webster_full: JES'UIT, n. One of the Society of Jesus, founded by Ignatius Loyola; a society remarkable for their cunning in propagating their principles.
Hence, a crafty person; an intriguer.
JESUIT'IC, JESUIT'ICAL, a. Designing; cunning; deceitful.
JES'UITISM, n. The arts, principles and practices of the Jesuits.
scriptures: And through covetousness shall they with feigned words make merchandise of you: whose judgment now of a long time lingereth not, and their damnation slumbereth not.
But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.
Mat 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Jer 6:14
They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
corruption_summary: The name of Jesus is worn as a badge, and Paul feared a mind corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary will not pretend every Jesuit was a villain, and it will not pretend the Protestant charge was a mood. Equivocation, mental reservation, probabilism, and the defence of a deposing pope were taught, printed, and denied in the same century. Matthew 5:37 is not a style preference. Yea, yea; nay, nay. A casuistry that can make a spoken yes sit beside a reserved no has already left the mountain.

Second Corinthians 11:3 is the verse the controversy is about. Subtilty against simplicity. An order can be learned, disciplined, courageous in missions, and still be a school of that subtilty. The test is not the courage. It is whether the mind is kept in the simplicity that is in Christ, or trained to manage Him.

The Protestant copy is Jesuitism without the Latin: platforms that heal slightly, Peace, peace, when the command has not been kept. Jeremiah 6:14 is older than Loyola. Try the spirits. The badge is not the try.
roots_summary: Society of Jesus, 1540; Greek haplotes (G572), simplicity; panourgia (G3834), subtilty, craft.
roots_lines: Latin Societas Iesu — the Society of Jesus; founded 1540.
Greek haplotes (G572) — simplicity, singleness; 2 Corinthians 11:3, the simplicity that is in Christ.
Greek panourgia (G3834) — craft, subtilty; 2 Corinthians 11:3, the serpent's subtilty.
usage: “The simplicity that is in Christ” — the thing subtilty corrupts.
“Yea, yea; Nay, nay” — against mental reservation.
“Try the spirits” — the badge is not the try.

pos: n. & adj. (a beggar; in church history, a friar of an order that lives by begging rather than by endowments)
etymology: Latin mendicans, begging, from mendicus, a beggar. Webster keeps both the common beggar and the mendicant orders. The Franciscans and Dominicans were founded as mendicants: poverty as a rule, alms as a living. The dictionary honours the protest against fat monasteries and will not make begging a gospel.
biblical_def: A mendicant lives by asking. The New Testament knows poor saints, and it does not make a vow of begging the mark of holiness. Paul laboured: “Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me” (Act 20:34). He would not be chargeable: “Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you” (2Th 3:8). The rule for the idle is sharper: “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10). And the contentment Scripture commends is food and raiment, not a theatre of want: “And having food and raiment let us be therewith content” (1Ti 6:8). The Lord sent the seventy without purse, and the same Lord had Judas keep a bag. Poverty can be wisdom. A rule that binds a man to beg as holiness is a different thing: “But godliness with contentment is great gain” (1Ti 6:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mendicant as begging, and, as a noun, a beggar; also one of the begging friars of the Roman church.
webster_full: MEND'ICANT, a. [L. mendicans, from mendico, to beg.]
Begging; poor to a state of beggary.
MEND'ICANT, n. A beggar; one that makes it his business to beg alms; one of the begging friars of the Romish church.
MENDIC'ITY, n. The state of begging; the life of a beggar.
scriptures: Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me.
Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you:
For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.
And having food and raiment let us be therewith content.
But godliness with contentment is great gain.
corruption_summary: Begging is made a higher holiness, and Paul ministered with his own hands that he might not be chargeable.
corruption_paragraphs: The Spiritual Franciscans are already on this shelf, and they show the fork. A protest against a rich church can be righteous, and a vow that turns poverty into a sacrament can bind where God did not. First Timothy 6:8 is contentment, not a performance of want. Food and raiment. The rest is not a second baptism.

Second Thessalonians 3 is written to a church, not to a monastery, and it still judges the theatre. If any would not work, neither should he eat. An order that makes not-working a rule of perfection has inverted the apostle. Paul wrought night and day. The friar who begs as if begging were holiness has chosen a different apostle.

Acts 20:34 is the elder's pattern in the same speech that warns of wolves. These hands. A clergy that cannot say that, and a mendicancy that will not, are two ways to make the gospel look like a living. Godliness with contentment is great gain. The gain is not the alms.
roots_summary: Latin mendicare, to beg; Greek kopiáo (G2872), to labour; autarkeia (G841), contentment.
roots_lines: Latin mendicans — begging; the mendicant orders live by alms.
Greek kopiao (G2872) — to labour unto weariness; Acts 20:34, these hands have ministered; 2 Thessalonians 3:8, wrought with labour.
Greek autarkeia (G841) — contentment, sufficiency; 1 Timothy 6:6, godliness with contentment.
usage: “These hands have ministered” — Paul's mendicancy was work.
“If any would not work, neither should he eat” — a rule, not a vibe.
“Food and raiment” — contentment, not a vow of begging.

pos: n. (the Order of Preachers, founded by Dominic; mendicant, and later the school of Aquinas and of the Inquisition's most famous theologians)
etymology: From Dominic of Caleruega (d. 1221), Latin Dominicus, of the Lord. The Order of Preachers was founded to preach against the Cathars, took a mendicant rule, and became the house of Thomas Aquinas and of a long line of inquisitors. The dictionary will take Aquinas's help where he is a servant of the text, and it will not baptize the rack.
biblical_def: Dominicans are preachers by name. The New Testament's preacher is a man under a word, not a man with a tribunal. “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine” (2Ti 4:2). The same Paul had already said how the word is to be handled: “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15). The weapons are not fleshly: “For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2Co 10:4). And the servant of the Lord must not strive: “And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient” (2Ti 2:24). Jude's charge is to contend for the faith, not to invent a court for it: “that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3). An order can preach and still forget which weapons those are.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Dominican as a friar of the order of St. Dominic, called also predicants and preaching friars.
webster_full: DOMIN'ICAN, n. One of the order of St. Dominic; a Dominican friar; called also a jacobin, predicant, or preaching friar.
DOMIN'ICAN, a. Belonging to that order.
The order was mendicant, devoted to preaching, and later closely tied to the Inquisition and to Thomist theology.
scriptures: Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient,
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: Preaching is joined to a carnal weapon, and Paul said the weapons of our warfare are not carnal.
corruption_paragraphs: The Order of Preachers has a right name. Second Timothy 4:2 is that name's job: preach the word, reprove, rebuke, exhort, with doctrine. A church that will not do that work will envy anyone who will. The dictionary is not against Dominicans for preaching. It is against the moment the pulpit borrowed the magistrate's knife and called it the cure of souls.

Second Corinthians 10:4 is the verse the Inquisition could not keep. Not carnal. Mighty through God. Strong holds come down by truth, not by a confession extracted in a cellar. Second Timothy 2:24 is the tone: gentle, apt to teach, patient. A theology that needs a rack to finish its sentences has already lost the argument it meant to save.

Jude 1:3 still stands. Contend for the faith once delivered. Contend is not a warrant for a holy office of pain. Aquinas may still be read with profit, and the rack is still a sin. The dictionary will not let a useful school wash a carnal weapon.
roots_summary: Latin Ordo Praedicatorum; Greek kerusso (G2784), to preach; machomai is what the servant must not do.
roots_lines: Latin Ordo Praedicatorum — the Order of Preachers; Dominic, 1216.
Greek kerusso (G2784) — to herald, preach; 2 Timothy 4:2, preach the word.
Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut straight; 2 Timothy 2:15, rightly dividing the word of truth.
usage: “Preach the word” — the right half of the name.
“The weapons of our warfare are not carnal” — the half the Inquisition dropped.
“Must not strive” — gentle, apt to teach, patient.

pos: n. (the teaching of Michael Baius of Louvain, condemned at Rome in 1567, which pressed Augustinian inability so far that Rome smelled Protestantism and Baius would not leave Rome)
etymology: From Michael Baius (de Bay, 1513–1589). Baius taught that fallen man has no purely natural good, that concupiscence is already sin, and that grace is owed to unfallen nature. Pius V condemned a long list of his propositions. Jansen would later drink from the same well. The dictionary notes the irony: Rome condemned a man for sounding like Augustine, and would not become Protestant for having been right about the fall.
biblical_def: Baianism is a school's name for a cluster of sentences about the fall. The Bible's sentences are older. “Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me” (Psa 51:5). Paul will not leave a purely natural good standing: “For I know that in me (that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing” (Rom 7:18). The mind of the flesh is not under-equipped. It is enmity: “Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be” (Rom 8:7). And the state is death, not a wound: “And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins” (Eph 2:1). Grace is not a wage owed to a nature that almost made it. It is mercy to the dead: “Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;)” (Eph 2:5). Baius saw the inability. He would not follow it out of Babylon.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for the school-name. Baianism is the Louvain teaching condemned in 1567 for pressing the fall and grace in ways Rome would not bear.
webster_full: BAIANISM, from Michael Baius (de Bay) of Louvain. Historical theological name, not an 1828 English headword.
Fallen man has no morally good act from nature alone; concupiscence is sin; grace is not a mere aid to an intact will.
Condemned by Pius V (1567). Later fed Jansenism.
The biblical cargo is Romans 7:18 and Ephesians 2:1,5. The tragedy is that Baius would not leave the see that condemned the sentences.
scriptures: Psa 51:5
Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me.
Rom 7:18
For I know that in me (that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing: for to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not.
Rom 8:7
Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be.
Eph 2:1
And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins;
Eph 2:5
Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;)
corruption_summary: Inability is either denied so that nature can still choose God, or admitted and then left inside a church that condemns the admission.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome's condemnation of Baius is a historical confession. The propositions that frightened Pius V are, many of them, the fall as Paul wrote it. In my flesh dwelleth no good thing. The carnal mind is not subject, neither indeed can be. A see that needs a leftover natural good to keep its synergy intact will have to call Augustine a problem.

Baius's own error, where it is real, is the other half of the irony. He would not become a Protestant. He recanted on paper and kept teaching in the same faculty. Ephesians 2:5 is not a Louvain thesis to be managed. By grace ye are saved. A man who sees the death and stays at an altar that sells a repair has seen only half the verse.

The modern copy is softer and more common. Churches that will preach inability on Sunday and invite a decision that nature can still make on Monday are Baius without the Latin, and without his excuse. Dead men are quickened. They are not coached.
roots_summary: Michael Baius, Louvain; Hebrew avon (H5771), iniquity; Greek sarx (G4561), flesh; nekros (G3498), dead.
roots_lines: Baius (de Bay), 1513–1589; condemned 1567; a well Jansen later drank.
Greek sarx (G4561) — flesh; Romans 7:18, in my flesh dwelleth no good thing.
Greek nekros (G3498) — dead; Ephesians 2:1, 5, dead in sins, quickened by grace.
usage: “In my flesh dwelleth no good thing” — the sentence Rome could not bear.
“Neither indeed can be” — not, can be with a nudge.
“Dead in trespasses” — then quickened, not coached.

pos: n. phrase (the penny paid to Rome; an annual tax claimed for St. Peter and collected for the pope)
etymology: English Peter's pence, from the medieval denarius Sancti Petri: a penny a hearth, claimed for the apostle and paid to the see. England paid it until the Reformation stopped the export. The name borrows Peter. The purse is Rome's.
biblical_def: Peter's pence is a tax that wears an apostle's name. The New Testament's Peter would not take silver for the gift. “But Peter said unto him, Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money” (Act 8:20). The Lord had already sent the twelve without a collecting plate for the office: “freely ye have received, freely give” (Mat 10:8). When the temple tax came due, He paid it by a miracle and still called the sons free: “Notwithstanding, lest we should offend them, go thou to the sea” (Mat 17:27), after “Then are the children free” (Mat 17:26). Paul would not make the gospel chargeable where it would darken the offer: “What is my reward then? Verily that, when I preach the gospel, I may make the gospel of Christ without charge” (1Co 9:18). And Peter himself forbids filthy lucre in the elder: “Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2). A penny claimed in Peter's name for a Roman court has to get past Peter's own mouth.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Peter-pence as a tax formerly paid by the English to the pope, being a penny for every house, payable at Lammas day.
webster_full: PE'TER-PENCE, n. A tax formerly paid by the English to the pope; being a penny for every house, payable at Lammas day. It was called also the see-penny, Rome-scot, and hearth-penny.
The tax was claimed as due to St. Peter and paid to the bishop of Rome.
It was abolished in England at the Reformation.
scriptures: Act 8:20
But Peter said unto him, Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money.
Mat 10:8
Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, raise the dead, cast out devils: freely ye have received, freely give.
Peter saith unto him, Of strangers. Jesus saith unto him, Then are the children free.
What is my reward then? Verily that, when I preach the gospel, I may make the gospel of Christ without charge, that I abuse not my power in the gospel.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
corruption_summary: An apostle's name is put on a levy, and Peter told Simon the gift of God is not purchased with money.
corruption_paragraphs: The medieval claim was modest: a penny a hearth, St. Peter's due. Acts 8:20 is not modest about that kind of sentence. Thy money perish with thee. The gift of God is not a line item. A see that collects in Peter's name for its own court has already answered the apostle who would not sell what he did not own.

Matthew 10:8 is the mission charge, not a fundraising brochure. Freely ye have received, freely give. First Corinthians 9:18 is Paul declining a right so the offer would not look like a fee. Peter's pence does the opposite. It makes the church of Rome a destination for coin, and calls the coin piety.

The Protestant copy is a ministry that cannot preach without a product. First Peter 5:2 still forbids filthy lucre in the elder. The flock is fed, not billed for the chair. A penny was never the scandal. The name on the penny was.
roots_summary: Medieval Latin denarius Sancti Petri; Greek dorean (G1432), freely; aischrokerdos (G146), for filthy lucre.
roots_lines: Latin denarius Sancti Petri — St. Peter's penny; English Peter's pence, Rome-scot, hearth-penny.
Greek dorean (G1432) — freely, as a gift; Matthew 10:8, freely ye have received, freely give.
Greek aischrokerdos (G146) — greedy of filthy lucre; 1 Peter 5:2, not for filthy lucre.
usage: “Thy money perish with thee” — Peter, on buying the gift.
“Freely ye have received, freely give” — not, remit a penny to Rome.
“Not for filthy lucre” — said by the man whose name is on the tax.

pos: n. (Luther's name for those who denied the bodily presence in the Supper, especially the Swiss; later a Lutheran school-term for Zwinglians and the Reformed)
etymology: From sacrament, used as a slur by Luther after Marburg (1529): men who leave only a sacrament, a sign, and will not have is mean is. The dictionary will not take the slur as a verdict. It will take the argument. Zwingli is already on this shelf. This page is the name Luther gave the other side of the table.
biblical_def: Sacramentarians, in Lutheran speech, are the men who will not say the bread is the body in Luther's sense. The New Testament's own words are the table, not the slur. “this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me” (1Co 11:24). The same apostle calls the eating a communion: “The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?” (1Co 10:16). And he still calls it bread when he warns: “For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” (1Co 11:26). The Lord had already said the flesh profits nothing if it is chewed as a charm: “It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life” (John 6:63). Luke keeps both the thanksgiving and the remembrance: “this do in remembrance of me” (Luk 22:19). The Reformed deny a local body in the elements. They do not deny the communion.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sacramentarian as one who differs from the Romish church in regard to the sacraments, a term applied by Catholics to Protestants, and sometimes to a particular class of Protestants.
webster_full: SACRAMENTA'RIAN, n. One who differs from the Romish church in regard to the sacraments; a term applied by the Romanists to Protestants.
The word has been applied also to those who deny the real presence, as the Zwinglians.
In Lutheran controversy after Marburg, a slur for the Swiss and the Reformed.
scriptures: And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me.
The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
John 6:63
It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.
And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me.
corruption_summary: Either the sign is emptied into a mere reminder, or the slur is used to make the Reformed deny the thing they confess: communion of the body and blood.
corruption_paragraphs: Luther wanted is to do more work than a sign can do, and he called the other men sacramentarians as if they had only a ceremony left. First Corinthians 10:16 is why that will not stick. Communion of the blood. Communion of the body. The 1689 will say worthy receivers spiritually receive and feed upon Christ crucified, and not after a corporal or carnal manner. That is not an empty table. It is a refusal to lock the ascended body into the baker's loaf.

The opposite error earns the slur. A memorialism that will only say remember, and will not say communion, has dropped half of Paul. First Corinthians 11:26 is shew the Lord's death, and 10:16 is participation. A church that treats the Supper as an object lesson with crackers has become what Luther feared, and the fear does not make Luther's metaphysics true.

John 6:63 is not a Zwinglian trick. It is the Lord's own brake on a carnal eating. The flesh profiteth nothing. The words are spirit and life. Marburg failed to agree, and the church still has to eat. The dictionary's table is the Reformed table: real communion, no local enclosure, no empty sign.
roots_lines: Luther's slur after Marburg, 1529; aimed at Zwingli and then at the Reformed.
Greek koinonia (G2842) — communion, participation; 1 Corinthians 10:16, communion of the blood, of the body.
Greek anamnesis (G364) — remembrance; 1 Corinthians 11:24, Luke 22:19, this do in remembrance.
usage: “Is it not the communion of the body” — not an empty sign.
“Eat this bread” — Paul still calls it bread.
“The flesh profiteth nothing” — the Lord's own brake.

pos: n. (favor to nephews and kin in giving office; in Rome, the papal habit of enriching a family out of the church)
etymology: Italian nepotismo, from Latin nepos, nephew, grandson. The Renaissance papacy made the nephew a prince. Webster already has the word: fondness for nephews, and undue patronage of relations. The Bible's word for the thing is respect of persons in the gate.
biblical_def: Nepotism is office given to blood. Scripture's gate is not a family business. “Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty” (Lev 19:15). Jehoshaphat charged the judges the same way: “Take heed what ye do: for ye judge not for man, but for the Lord” (2Ch 19:6). The New Testament's elder is not a nephew. He is a man whose house is ruled, not a house that rules the church: “One that ruleth well his own house” (1Ti 3:4). And the warning against respect of persons is still on the door: “My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons” (Jas 2:1). Deuteronomy had already named the bribe that blinds: “thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift” (Deu 16:19). A see that makes a boy a cardinal has not found a loophole in that verse. It has illustrated it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines nepotism as favoritism shown to nephews and other relations; nomination to office on account of relationship, regardless of merit.
webster_full: NEP'OTISM, n. [L. nepos, a nephew.]
Favoritism shown to nephews and other relations; patronage bestowed on account of relationship, regardless of merit.
A word originally used of the popes who raised their nephews to wealth and dignity.
scriptures: Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour.
And said to the judges, Take heed what ye do: for ye judge not for man, but for the LORD, who is with you in the judgment.
One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity;
Jas 2:1
My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons.
Thou shalt not wrest judgment; thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift: for a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise, and pervert the words of the righteous.
corruption_summary: Blood is made a qualification, and the gate was told not to honour the person of the mighty.
corruption_paragraphs: The papal nephew is the textbook case, and the textbook is not only Roman. Protestant boards have sons and sons-in-law enough. First Timothy 3:4 is a man who rules his house, not a house that inherits the pulpit. An elder's son may be called. He may not be owed.

James 2:1 is written to a church that had already learned to seat the gold ring. Respect of persons is not a Renaissance vice. It is the ordinary sin of a people who love the Lord of glory and still want a family in the chair. Leviticus 19:15 forbids it in both directions: do not honour the mighty, and do not make a mascot of the poor.

Deuteronomy 16:19 joins the gift and the respect. A nephew's red hat is a gift. It blinds. Second Chronicles 19:6 is the only safe fear in that room: ye judge not for man, but for the Lord. A church that cannot say that when the name is the pastor's will do the same thing Rome did, with worse Latin.
roots_summary: Latin nepos, nephew; Hebrew nakar / nasa panim, to respect persons; Greek prosopolepsia (G4382).
roots_lines: Italian nepotismo — the papal nephew as a political fact.
Hebrew idiom nasa panim — to lift the face, respect persons; Leviticus 19:15, Deuteronomy 16:19.
Greek prosopolepsia (G4382) — respect of persons; James 2:1, not with respect of persons.
usage: “Nor honour the person of the mighty” — even when the mighty is a nephew.
“Ye judge not for man, but for the Lord” — the only safe fear in that room.
“Not with respect of persons” — the faith of the Lord of glory.

pos: n. (the act of clothing a man with office; in controversy, the fight over who puts the ring and staff into a bishop's hand, emperor or pope)
etymology: Latin investire, to clothe, from in + vestis, a garment. Medieval bishops received ring and staff as the signs of office. The Investiture Controversy asked who may hand them over. The dictionary's question is older: who calls, and by what word.
biblical_def: Investiture is the clothing of a man with a charge. The New Testament's clothing is hands and a word, not a prince's ring. “As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them” (Act 13:2). The church then obeyed: “And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away” (Act 13:3). Timothy's gift is tied to that laying on: “Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery” (1Ti 4:14). Paul reminds him again: “Wherefore I put thee in remembrance that thou stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands” (2Ti 1:6). And the warning is not about whose palace did the clothing: “Lay hands suddenly on no man” (1Ti 5:22). The controversy of the eleventh century was about a staff. The apostle's controversy is about a sudden hand.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines investiture as the action of giving possession, or livery of seizin; the right of giving possession of any manor, office or benefice.
webster_full: INVEST'ITURE, n. The action of giving possession, or livery of seizin, as the grant of land or of an office.
The right of giving possession of any manor, office or benefice.
In church history, the ceremony of conferring ring and staff, and the war over who may do it.
scriptures: Act 13:2
As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them.
Act 13:3
And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.
Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.
Wherefore I put thee in remembrance that thou stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands.
Lay hands suddenly on no man, neither be partaker of other men's sins: keep thyself pure.
corruption_summary: Office is treated as a property a prince or a pope may hand over, and Acts 13 starts with the Holy Ghost saying Separate me.
corruption_paragraphs: Canossa is a famous picture, and it can hide the real question. An emperor who staffs bishoprics as fiefs has made the church a department of the crown. A pope who then claims the only lawful hand has made the church a department of Rome. Acts 13:2 is neither. The Holy Ghost said, Separate me. The church fasted, laid hands, and sent. Investiture that does not begin there is a costume.

The Protestant copy is a board that calls a man because he is impressive, or a dynasty that treats the pulpit as real estate. First Timothy 5:22 is the brake. Lay hands suddenly on no man. Sudden is the word for a staff pressed into a favorite's palm. First Timothy 4:14 ties the gift to prophecy and the presbytery, not to a palace.

Second Timothy 1:6 is why the ceremony still matters. A real gift, a real putting on of hands. The dictionary is not against a public clothing. It is against a clothing that can be sold, inherited, or reversed by a better army. The Lord of the church still says Separate me, and He has not leased that sentence to a court.
roots_summary: Latin investire, to clothe; Greek epitithemi tas cheiras, to lay on hands; aphorizo (G873), to separate.
roots_lines: Latin investitura — the clothing with ring and staff; then the war over the hand that does it.
Greek aphorizo (G873) — to separate, set apart; Acts 13:2, Separate me Barnabas and Saul.
Greek epithesis ton cheiron — laying on of hands; 1 Timothy 4:14, 2 Timothy 1:6, 1 Timothy 5:22.
usage: “Separate me Barnabas and Saul” — the only safe beginning of a clothing.
“The laying on of the hands of the presbytery” — not of a palace.
“Lay hands suddenly on no man” — sudden is the favorite's staff.
